title: Climate-Driven Mass Redistribution and the Secular Evolution of Earth’s Rotation
content: Background: Anthropogenic climate change is altering the distribution of mass within the Earth system through accelerated melting of polar ice sheets, glacier retreat, and changes in terrestrial water storage and ocean mass. These processes affect Earth’s axial moment of inertia and may contribute to variations in its rotational period. The purpose of this study is to develop a simplified analytical framework for estimating how climate-driven mass redistribution influences Earth’s length of day (LOD), while identifying the assumptions and limitations of such estimates. Methods: We employ an analytical model based on conservation of Earth’s axial angular momentum to relate changes in its moment of inertia to variations in LOD. An assumed annual ice mass-loss rate of 5.0×1015kgyr−1 is used to estimate the rotational response. A geometrical redistribution factor accounts for the initial and final latitudes of transferred mass. Cumulative LOD changes are calculated over 1990–2025 under constant-rate assumptions. Results: The analytical model yields an idealized LOD increase of approximately 0.218msyr−1 for a unit geometrical redistribution factor. Under constant-rate assumptions, this corresponds to a cumulative increase of approximately 7.63ms between 1990 and 2025. The magnitude and sign of the rotational response depend on the geographical distribution of transferred mass. Conclusions: Climate-driven mass redistribution can influence Earth’s rotational period through changes in its axial moment of inertia. However, the calculated LOD variations are idealized sensitivity estimates rather than observationally verified anthropogenic trends. Quantitative attribution requires spatially resolved mass-transfer data, solid-Earth deformation models, and independent geodetic observations.
